steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper ConsPrompt, which adds contrastive learning over contrastive samples to few-shot prompt-based fine-tuning of language models. Cover background on prompt learning, its weaknesses, our motivation, and a short list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- LLMs as knowledge bases; prompt learning approaches
- Problems: prompt sensitivity, overfitting in few-shot
- Motivation: contrastive learning for knowledge activation
- Our model ConsPrompt
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- Background
  - LLMs + prompting strategies growing fast; PLMs as knowledge base / linguistic tool for few-shot learning (ChatGPT, LLAMA)
  - research focuses on prompting strategies and prompt learning methods to activate knowledge in PLMs
  - zhong et al.: OptiPrompt, factual probing with soft-prompt embedding
  - training strategies: fine-tuning prefix-prompt vs. independent prompt encoder; P-tuning, Prefix-tuning, Auto-prompt learning, Prompt-tuning
- Problems
  - small changes to prompt design -> very different results
  - prompt learning easily over-fits limited samples
  - activating LLMs in few-shot settings with different cognitive learning abilities and prompting strategies still an open question
- Motivation
  - humans also use different learning rules to activate knowledge from few samples, e.g. contrastive learning of different prompts and samples
  - we exploit fewer samples + multiple contrastive learning methods in prompt-based fine-tuning
- Our model (Fig. 1)
  - Fig. 1: token- and sentence-level attention of transformer models; more accurate token-level attention and contrastive learning can enhance LLMs
  - prompt-level and batch-level contrastive information of tokens
  - two negative sampling strategies + SBERT -> ConsPrompt
  - result: multiple contrastive learning effective in prompt-based fine-tuning; suitable negative sampling helps robustness
- Contributions
  - ConsPrompt: increases prompt's distinguishing ability on prompt-level and batch-level samples
  - two sampling strategies + SimCLR contrastive learning against overfitting in prompt learning
  - state-of-the-art performance, k-shot robustness on five representative few-shot tasks

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

With large language models (LLMs) and prompting strategies growing exponentially, pre-trained language models can now be used as a huge knowledge base or as a strong linguistic tool for few-shot learning, like ChatGPT and LLAMA. To activate the knowledge that is already embedded in PLMs, research is mainly concentrating on different prompting strategies and prompt learning methods, and zhong et al. put forward the OptiPrompt model for factual probing based on soft-prompt embedding. In terms of training strategies, prompt learning can be classified into fine-tuning of a prefix-prompt and fine-tuning of an independent prompt encoder, for example P-tuning, Prefix-tuning, Auto-prompt learning, and Prompt-tuning.

However, small changes in how the prompt is designed often make the results very different, and the prompt learning process also over-fits the limited samples easily. So how to use different cognitive learning abilities and prompting strategies to activate LLMs in few-shot settings is still a big question. Besides prompting strategies, humans can also use different learning rules to activate knowledge from few samples, like contrastive learning of different prompts and different samples. Motivated by this, we look at how to use fewer samples and several contrastive learning methods in prompt-based fine-tuning models.

- Our model (Fig. 1)
  - Fig. 1: token- and sentence-level attention in transformer models; better token-level attention + contrastive learning enhance LLMs
  - prompt-level and batch-level contrastive information of tokens
  - two negative sampling strategies + SBERT -> ConsPrompt
  - multiple contrastive learning works; negative sampling helps robustness
- Contributions
  - ConsPrompt: distinguishing ability on prompt-level and batch-level samples
  - two sampling strategies + SimCLR against overfitting
  - SOTA and k-shot robustness on five few-shot tasks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

With large language models (LLMs) and prompting strategies growing exponentially, pre-trained language models can now be used as a huge knowledge base or as a strong linguistic tool for few-shot learning, like ChatGPT and LLAMA. To activate the knowledge that is already embedded in PLMs, research is mainly concentrating on different prompting strategies and prompt learning methods, and zhong et al. put forward the OptiPrompt model for factual probing based on soft-prompt embedding. In terms of training strategies, prompt learning can be classified into fine-tuning of a prefix-prompt and fine-tuning of an independent prompt encoder, for example P-tuning, Prefix-tuning, Auto-prompt learning, and Prompt-tuning.

However, small changes in how the prompt is designed often make the results very different, and the prompt learning process also over-fits the limited samples easily. So how to use different cognitive learning abilities and prompting strategies to activate LLMs in few-shot settings is still a big question. Besides prompting strategies, humans can also use different learning rules to activate knowledge from few samples, like contrastive learning of different prompts and different samples. Motivated by this, we look at how to use fewer samples and several contrastive learning methods in prompt-based fine-tuning models.

Fig. 1 shows the token-level and sentence-level attention mechanism of a transformer-based model, and it shows that LLMs can be made more effective by more accurate token-level attention and by contrastive learning methods. So we use the prompt-level and the batch-level contrastive information of tokens to strengthen the few-shot prompt-based learning task, and we also use two negative sampling strategies and the SBERT model to help the contrastive prompt learning model, which we call ConsPrompt. Our results show that multiple contrastive learning is effective in prompt-based fine-tuning. Also, the robustness of prompt-based learning can be improved with suitable negative sampling strategies. Our main contributions are:

- We propose a new contrastive prompt model, ConsPrompt, which increases the prompt's ability to distinguish prompt-level and batch-level samples.

- We introduce two sampling strategies and the SimCLR contrastive learning method to reduce the overfitting that is widespread in the prompt learning process.

- The results show state-of-the-art performance and k-shot robustness on five representative few-shot tasks.

steps.text:
## Introduction

With large language models (LLMs) and prompting strategies growing exponentially, pre-trained language models can now be used as a huge knowledge base or as a strong linguistic tool for few-shot learning [1], like ChatGPT and LLAMA. To activate the knowledge that is already embedded in PLMs, research is mainly concentrating on different prompting strategies and prompt learning methods [2], and zhong et al. put forward the OptiPrompt model for factual probing based on soft-prompt embedding [3]. In terms of training strategies, prompt learning can be classified into fine-tuning of a prefix-prompt and fine-tuning of an independent prompt encoder, for example P-tuning [4], Prefix-tuning [5], Auto-prompt learning [6], and Prompt-tuning [7].

However, small changes in how the prompt is designed often make the results very different, and the prompt learning process also over-fits the limited samples easily. So how to use different cognitive learning abilities and prompting strategies to activate LLMs in few-shot settings is still a big question [8,4,7]. Besides prompting strategies, humans can also use different learning rules to activate knowledge from few samples [9], like contrastive learning of different prompts and different samples. Motivated by this, we look at how to use fewer samples and several contrastive learning methods in prompt-based fine-tuning models.

Fig. 1 shows the token-level and sentence-level attention mechanism of a transformer-based model, and it shows that LLMs can be made more effective by more accurate token-level attention and by contrastive learning methods. So we use the prompt-level and the batch-level contrastive information of tokens to strengthen the few-shot prompt-based learning task, and we also use two negative sampling strategies and the SBERT [10] model to help the contrastive prompt learning model, which we call ConsPrompt. Our results show that multiple contrastive learning is effective in prompt-based fine-tuning. Also, the robustness of prompt-based learning can be improved with suitable negative sampling strategies. Our main contributions are:

- We propose a new contrastive prompt model, ConsPrompt, which increases the prompt's ability to distinguish prompt-level and batch-level samples.

- We introduce two sampling strategies and the SimCLR contrastive learning method to reduce the overfitting that is widespread in the prompt learning process.

- The results show state-of-the-art performance and k-shot robustness on five representative few-shot tasks.

References:
[1] Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever, et al., “Language models are unsupervised multitask learners,” OpenAI blog , vol. 1, no. 8, pp. 9, 2019.
[2] Andrea Madotto, Zhaojiang Lin, Genta Indra Winata, and Pascale Fung, “Few-shot bot: Prompt-based learning for dialogue systems,” CoRR , vol. abs/2110.08118, 2021.
[3] Zexuan Zhong, Dan Friedman, and Danqi Chen, “Factual probing is [mask]: Learning vs. learning to recall,” 2021.
[4] Xiao Liu, Yanan Zheng, Zhengxiao Du, Ming Ding, Yujie Qian, Zhilin Yang, and Jie Tang, “Gpt understands, too,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.10385 , 2021.
[5] Xiang Lisa Li and Percy Liang, “Prefix-tuning: Optimizing continuous prompts for generation,” in Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers) , Online, Aug. 2021, pp. 4582–4597, Association for Computational Linguistics.
[6] Taylor Shin, Yasaman Razeghi, Robert L Logan IV, Eric Wallace, and Sameer Singh, “Autoprompt: Eliciting knowledge from language models with automatically generated prompts,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.15980 , 2020.
[7] Timo Schick and Hinrich Schütze, “Exploiting cloze-questions for few-shot text classification and natural language inference,” in Proceedings of the 16th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Main Volume , Online, Apr. 2021, pp. 255–269, Association for Computational Linguistics.
[8] Adam Roberts, Colin Raffel, and Noam Shazeer, “How much knowledge can you pack into the parameters of a language model?,” in Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) , Online, Nov. 2020, pp. 5418–5426, Association for Computational Linguistics.
[9] Yangyan Xu, Fangfang Yuan, Cong Cao, Majing Su, Yuhai Lu, and Yanbing Liu, “A contrastive self-distillation bert with kernel alignment-based inference,” in International Conference on Computational Science . Springer, 2023, pp. 553–565.
[10] Nils Reimers and Iryna Gurevych, “Sentence-bert: Sentence embeddings using siamese bert-networks,” in Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP) , 2019, pp. 3982–3992.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

With the exponential growth of large language models (LLMs) and prompting strategies, pre-trained language models can now serve as a huge knowledge base or a superior linguistic tool for few-shot learning [1], like ChatGPT and LLAMA. To activate the existing knowledge embedded in PLMs, research mainly concentrates on different prompting strategies and prompt learning methods [2], and zhong et al. put forward the OptiPrompt model for factual probing based on soft-prompt embedding [3]. In terms of training strategies, prompt learning can be classified into the fine-tuning of a prefix-prompt and the fine-tuning of an independent prompt encoder, such as P-tuning [4], Prefix-tuning [5], Auto-prompt learning [6], and Prompt-tuning [7].

However, subtle changes in prompt design often make results widely different, and the prompt learning process also easily over-fits the limited samples. Therefore, utilizing different cognitive learning abilities and prompting strategies to activate LLMs in few-shot settings is still a considerable question [8,4,7]. In addition to prompting strategies, humans can also use different learning rules to realize knowledge activation based on few samples [9], like contrastive learning of different prompts and different samples. Motivated by this, we explore how to use fewer samples and multiple contrastive learning methods in prompt-based fine-tuning models.

As shown in Fig. 1, the token- and sentence-level attention mechanism of a transformer-based model reveals that the effectiveness of LLMs can be enhanced by more accurate token-level attention and contrastive learning methods. Therefore, we utilize the prompt-level and batch-level contrastive information of tokens to strengthen the few-shot prompt-based learning task, and two negative sampling strategies and the SBERT [10] model are also used to facilitate the contrastive prompt learning model, ConsPrompt. Our results show the effectiveness of multiple contrastive learning in prompt-based fine-tuning, and that the robustness of prompt-based learning can be empowered with suitable negative sampling strategies. The main contributions are:

- We propose a novel contrastive prompt model, ConsPrompt, for increasing the prompt's distinguishing ability on prompt-level and batch-level samples.

- Two sampling strategies and the SimCLR contrastive learning method are introduced to alleviate the widespread overfitting phenomenon in the prompt learning process.

- The results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and show k-shot robustness on five representative few-shot tasks.

References:
[1] Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever, et al., “Language models are unsupervised multitask learners,” OpenAI blog , vol. 1, no. 8, pp. 9, 2019.
[2] Andrea Madotto, Zhaojiang Lin, Genta Indra Winata, and Pascale Fung, “Few-shot bot: Prompt-based learning for dialogue systems,” CoRR , vol. abs/2110.08118, 2021.
[3] Zexuan Zhong, Dan Friedman, and Danqi Chen, “Factual probing is [mask]: Learning vs. learning to recall,” 2021.

[6] Taylor Shin, Yasaman Razeghi, Robert L Logan IV, Eric Wallace, and Sameer Singh, “Autoprompt: Eliciting knowledge from language models with automatically generated prompts,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.15980 , 2020.
[7] Timo Schick and Hinrich Schütze, “Exploiting cloze-questions for few-shot text classification and natural language inference,” in Proceedings of the 16th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Main Volume , Online, Apr. 2021, pp. 255–269, Association for Computational Linguistics.
